client: I've been really stressed out lately about my grades and this scholarship I'm on. Last semester I got a pretty bad mark on my final project, and now I can't stop thinking about what happens if I mess up again this term and lose the funding. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the pressure is just... real, you know? It's not like therapy can make my professors grade differently.
therapist: That sounds like a really heavy weight to carry — the fear of losing something so important, on top of already feeling like you stumbled last semester. You're right that I can't change how your professors grade, but what I *can* help with is that loop of "what if I mess up again" that's running in the background and draining your energy before you've even started. I'm curious — when that thought shows up, what does it tend to make you do, or avoid doing?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, when that thought shows up, I just kind of... freeze. Like I'll sit down to start an assignment and then suddenly I'm scrolling my phone for an hour because opening the document feels like the moment everything could go wrong. It's easier to not start than to start and confirm that I'm actually not as capable as I'm supposed to be.
therapist: What you just described — avoiding the document to avoid the verdict — makes so much sense as a short-term escape, but it sounds like part of you already knows it's keeping you stuck in that fear rather than moving through it. That thought, *"starting will confirm I'm not capable,"* is doing a lot of work against you; it's treating one bad grade as proof of something permanent about you, rather than just one outcome. What do you think it would mean about you *if* you did open the document and it turned out to be harder than expected?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it would mean I was right all along — that I really am struggling and maybe not cut out for this level of work. And honestly, that scares me more than just not knowing, because at least right now I can still tell myself it might be fine. If I open it and it's as bad as I fear, I lose that last bit of hope I'm holding onto.
therapist: That "last bit of hope" you're protecting makes complete sense — but I want to gently point out that what you're actually holding onto isn't hope, it's *uncertainty*, and those feel very different. Real hope would be something like, "I've struggled before and found a way through" — and I wonder if somewhere in your history, there's evidence of exactly that, even if it's hard to see right now. Can you think of a time when something felt beyond you at first, but you managed it anyway?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying about hope versus uncertainty, and honestly, that distinction kind of stings a little because I think you might be right. But when I try to think of a time I managed something that felt impossible... I mean, I got through my parents' divorce when I was a teenager, and I thought that would break me, but it didn't. I just don't know if that counts, because back then I didn't really have a choice, I just survived it — it's not like I actually handled it well.
therapist: You just offered up something really significant — surviving your parents' divorce as a teenager — and then immediately moved to take it away from yourself by saying it "doesn't count." But getting through something that felt like it might break you *is* handling it, even if it looked messy from the inside. I'm curious what you think "handling it well" would have looked like, because I wonder if your standard for what counts as coping might be set impossibly high for past-you *and* present-you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess "handling it well" would have looked like... not falling apart, not isolating myself, not failing two of my classes that semester. Like, I picture someone who just keeps going normally, maybe talks to a counselor or their friends, doesn't make everything worse. But even saying that out loud, I can kind of hear how that sounds — like I'm describing a robot, not a real teenager whose family was imploding.
therapist: You just caught yourself in real time — describing an impossible standard and then recognizing it sounds like a robot, not a human being in pain — and that's actually a really important moment of clarity. It sounds like part of you has been measuring teenage-you, and maybe current-you, against someone who doesn't exist. I'm wondering if that same impossible standard is part of what makes opening that document feel so terrifying right now — like anything less than perfect confirms the worst, rather than just confirming you're human.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I think you're right that the standard is impossible, and I can even hear myself saying it out loud and knowing it's unreasonable. But knowing that doesn't actually make opening the document feel any less terrifying, you know? Like, my brain understands what you're saying, but my stomach still drops every time I even think about clicking on it.
therapist: That gap between *knowing* and *feeling* is one of the most frustrating parts of being human — your mind can hold the logic while your body is still bracing for impact, and both of those things are real. What you're describing is actually really common in anxiety: insight doesn't automatically switch off the alarm system, which is why we'd want to work with the feeling directly, not just the thought. I'm wondering — when your stomach drops at the thought of clicking, what's the very first thing your body wants to do in that moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: When my stomach drops, the first thing I want to do is just... close the laptop and walk away, or find something else to do — anything to not have to deal with it. It's like my whole body is saying "nope, not today" before I've even consciously decided anything. I guess I've gotten pretty good at finding distractions so I don't have to sit with that feeling.
therapist: Your body has basically built an automatic escape hatch, and it sounds like it's become so practiced that it kicks in before you even have a say — that's not a character flaw, that's just a very well-trained protection system. The tricky part is that every time you walk away, it teaches your nervous system that the laptop *was* actually dangerous, which makes the next time feel even harder. I'm wondering if we could think together about what it might look like to stay with that "nope" feeling for just a little longer — not to force yourself through it, but to gently show your body that the drop in your stomach isn't the same as actual danger.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me gets it logically — like, yes, the laptop is not going to physically hurt me. But when that "nope" feeling hits, it doesn't feel like a small thing I can just sit with — it feels like this wall of dread that kind of takes over my whole chest, and I honestly can't imagine just... staying there in it. What would that even look like, because I feel like I'd just be torturing myself for no reason?
therapist: That wall of dread in your chest sounds genuinely overwhelming, and I want to be clear — I'm not suggesting you white-knuckle your way through it or just suffer for the sake of it. What "staying with it" would actually look like is much smaller than that: maybe it's keeping the laptop open for just 60 seconds while you breathe, not to work, just to let your body learn that the dread peaks and then *moves* rather than swallowing you whole. Would it feel any different if the goal wasn't "open the document and work" but just "sit near the scary thing and survive it for one minute"?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I mean... when you put it that way, it sounds almost manageable, but I'm not sure my brain will actually buy into the "just sit near it" framing once I'm in the moment. Like, the second that laptop is open, even if I'm telling myself I don't have to work, some part of me is going to start screaming that I should be doing something, and then I'll feel guilty for not doing it. It's like there's no neutral ground with this stuff — it's either "I'm working" or "I'm failing."
therapist: That "working or failing" split is such a painful place to live — there's no room in it to just *be* a person who's doing their best. And I notice that even as you're describing something that sounds almost manageable, there's a real heaviness in how you're sitting with it, like part of you is already bracing for the moment it falls apart. I'm curious about that voice that starts screaming you "should" be doing something — whose voice does that sound like, and where do you think it learned that rest or neutral ground equals failure?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. I think... it sounds like my dad, maybe? He was never mean about it, but he just always had this quiet disappointment when I wasn't productive, like resting was something you had to earn and I never quite earned it enough. And now I can't tell if that voice is him or just me, because it feels so automatic, like it's just the truth rather than something someone taught me.
therapist: What you just named — that you can't tell anymore if it's his voice or yours — is actually one of the most important things you've said today, because it points to exactly how deeply that belief got woven into who you think you are. The way you described it, "quiet disappointment," feels significant too — sometimes the messages that shape us most aren't the loud or cruel ones, but the ones we had to work hardest to interpret, always wondering if we were reading them right. I'm curious: if that voice *is* something he taught you rather than the truth, what would it mean for how you've been measuring yourself all this time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
